cards.text: The Teacher has watched good people get what the wicked deserve, and he admits no one can figure out the work done under the sun (Ecclesiastes 8:14, 17). So he takes ALL of it to heart. And he lands somewhere.

cards.question: After taking all this to heart, where does the Teacher say the righteous and the wise, and their deeds, are?
The Teacher says people know what lies ahead of them, whether love or hate.

cards.text: Then he lines people up in pairs: the righteous and the wicked, the clean and the unclean, the one who sacrifices and the one who does not. Total opposites, like me and a stamper that actually stamps straight.

cards.question: For all those pairs, the Teacher says there is a common ___ for the righteous and the wicked.

cards.text: He doesn't soften it one bit. He calls it an evil in everything done under the sun: one fate for everyone.

cards.question: The Teacher adds that while men are alive, their hearts are full of ___ and ___.

cards.text: And afterward, the Teacher says, they join the dead. But hold on, because he says there is hope for anyone who is among the living, and he backs it up with two animals.

cards.question: The Teacher says a dead lion is better than a live dog.

cards.text: A live dog, friend. Not a show dog, not a champion, just a dog that's STILL HERE, and the Teacher says that beats a lion.

cards.question: The Teacher explains what the living have going for them. What does he say the living know?

cards.text: THAT'S the edge, knowing you're gonna die?! Then the Teacher says the dead know nothing, and suddenly the living look like geniuses.

cards.question: Why does the Teacher say the dead have no further reward?

answers.text: The memory of them is forgotten

cards.question: The Teacher says the love, the hate and the envy of the dead have already vanished.

cards.text: And he says they will never again have a share in all that is done under the sun. Heavy stuff, friend, but stay with me, because the Teacher isn't done talking.
After all that talk about the dead, the Teacher turns to the living. And he starts with bread and wine.

cards.question: The Teacher says to go eat your bread with ___ and drink your wine with a cheerful heart.
Why does the Teacher say to eat your bread and drink your wine with a cheerful heart?

answers.text: God has already approved your works
The king has called for a feast

cards.text: Then he says, "Let your garments always be white, and never spare the oil for your head." Translation from the bakery: stop saving the good apron for a special day.

cards.question: Who does the Teacher say to enjoy life with?
The Teacher calls the life God has given you under the sun long and lasting.

cards.text: Nope, he calls those days fleeting, and he says this is your portion in life and in your labor under the sun. Then he turns to whatever you find to do with your hands.

cards.question: How does the Teacher say to do whatever you find to do with your hands?
Why does the Teacher say to do your work with all your might?

answers.text: In Sheol there is no work

cards.text: No work, no planning, no knowledge, no wisdom in Sheol, so if your oven's hot, BAKE. Then the Teacher says he saw something else under the sun, and it's about who comes out on top.

cards.question: The Teacher says the race goes to the swift and the battle goes to the strong.

cards.text: Same goes for bread, wealth and favor: they don't go to the wise, the intelligent and the skillful. It's like leaving for work early and STILL losing to the guy who left late and hit every green light.

cards.question: The Teacher says this is because time and ___ happen to all.

cards.text: And surely no man knows his time. Then the Teacher paints one more picture of how an evil time can fall on people.

cards.question: What does the Teacher say men ensnared in an evil time are like?

answers.text: Fish caught in a cruel net

cards.text: Birds trapped in a snare too, with an evil time that suddenly falls upon them. Nobody knows when their timer goes off, friend, which is exactly why I keep my ovens hot.

findings.problem: The Teacher appears for the first time here, but the card never says who he is. Ecclesiastes 1:1 calls him the Teacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: Ecclesiastes 8:14 says 'righteous men', but the card says 'good people'.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The joke 'like me and a stamper that actually stamps straight' says Papa Dorin still doesn't stamp straight. His backstory says he was renewed: 'His edges were sharp. His lines were clear.' The joke adds a new fact about his world that contradicts the backstory.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The two-blank card 'full of ___ and ___' asks the baker to guess the exact words of the line. Nothing told earlier lets the baker reason out 'madness' over 'pride', 'sorrow' or 'greed'. Card 6 also says 'an evil' right before, which points to the first blank.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: This card only reacts to the dog-and-lion line that card 9 already answered. It adds nothing new from the passage, so it doesn't move the baker forward.
The wrong answer 'They never asked for one' sounds flippant next to the serious tone of the other two answers.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Multiple choice makes up 5 of the 9 choice cards in this stop. True or false and fill in the blank have 2 each.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.
